newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK low-tax system separate but murky on handover.
newsitem.headline: HK low-tax system separate but murky on handover.

text.p: Beijing's autonomy pledge of "one country, two systems" means separate tax regimes after Hong Kong rejoins China next week, but not everything about future taxation in the territory is so clear.
"Article 108 of the Basic Law says that Hong Kong's tax system will remain separate after the handover," said Agnes Sin, deputy commissioner of Hong Kong's Inland Revenue Service (IRS).

The Basic Law, the territory's future constitution, states that Hong Kong -- taking a current low-tax policy as a reference -- shall "enact laws on its own concerning types of taxes, tax rates, tax reductions, allowances and exemptions, and other matters of taxation."

"The Basic Law enshrines Hong Kong as being a place that will have a separate tax system and will follow its standard policy of low rates and a stable, simple system, so there is really nothing that we expect to change," said Kaushal Tikku, partner at Price Waterhouse.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Individuals residing in Hong Kong pay a top tax rate of 15 percent, while companies are assessed at 16.5 percent.
Over the last several years, allowances have been increased so that Hong Kong taxes, both personal and corporate, rank among the lowest of developed economies, Tikku said.
Unlike some Asian neighbors, however, Hong Kong does not offer major tax breaks or tax holidays to some sectors.
Despite the simplicity of Hong Kong's tax system, there are still murky spots, particularly on tax treaties.
Tax experts said these areas could get even muddier once Hong Kong becomes a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China, at least in the short term.
Joseph Wong, partner at Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu, said Hong Kong's new status has left it in a peculiar tax position.

"Once Hong Kong becomes a part of China, we will not be able to have a tax treaty with China and it is difficult to have a tax treaty with the U.S., so how we deal with foreign people that work in Hong Kong and how Hong Kong people will be taxed in China is still open to question," he said.
Article 151 of the Basic Law allows Hong Kong to make arrangements with other states in economic matters, a clause that should include tax treaties.
"Article 151 does not specifically mention taxation, but it is very broad and there is no reason why tax would be excluded," said Sin of the IRS.
But analysts said that the SAR would have little to offer other countries in the way of tax treaties.
"Because taxes are so low and so narrow in their application it is difficult to do deals," said Ian Perkin, chief economist at the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.
With the exception of some minor tax arrangements specific to air operations, Hong Kong does not have any tax treaties with other countries now.

In the U.S., industry groups have been lobbying Washington to treat Hong Kong and China as "one country, one tax system," a change in treatment that could result in lower taxes for some U.S. companies that have subsidiaries in Hong Kong.
Because of Hong Kong's low tax rate, income of Hong Kong subsidiaries of U.S. companies in some cases is taxed by the American government in accordance with "anti-avoidance" rules.
The U.S. and other countries have double taxation treaties with China, but Hong Kong does not. Once it becomes part of China, it cannot have a tax treaty with the mainland.
Because of Hong Kong's unique position, Hong Kong people making money in China may pay higher taxes than Americans or Singaporeans, for example, which benefit from tax treaties.
"With Hong Kong becoming part of China and more and more people and companies working in both China and Hong Kong, there is a danger that more people could be taxed twice," said Perkin.
Hong Kong does not tax income earned on the mainland as long as there is evidence that taxes were paid in China.
China's State Administration of Tax also is aware of the double taxation problem and is studying it, Perkin said.
Hong Kong's IRS is not currently involved in talks with China's tax authorities, but Sin said she expected the two bodies to consider the double taxation issue after the handover.
